learning_outcomes.text: Students learn how problems can be modeled by suitable logical systems.
Students master the syntax and semantics of various logical systems and can use them.
Students know several classical logical calculi and can perform them.
Students have developed a basic understanding of logic programming and can express simple facts using Prolog programs.
Students know basic concepts of probability theory such as random variables, both discrete and continuous, and can apply them confidently.
Students master the determination of moments, such as the expected value and variance, in the discrete case using the technique of z-transformation.
Students learn various distributions important for computer science, such as the Binomial, Geometric, Poisson, Uniform, Exponential, and Normal distributions, and can apply them confidently.
Students are able to implement the presented techniques using the computer algebra system Sage in Python.

syllabus_topics: Logical methods in modern computer science applications
Diverse use of random bits for efficient algorithms
Logic-based query languages for information extraction from databases
Formal verification of software and hardware using logical specification languages and algorithms
Automated reasoning methods in artificial intelligence based on formal logic
Formal foundations of modern logics with a focus on computer science applications
Formalization of syntax and semantics for each logic
Modeling computer science scenarios in logical systems
Algorithms and calculi for unsatisfiability and entailment relation
Solutions to central computer science problems using random bits
Acceleration of algorithms with random bits
Elegant analysis of correctness and runtime with random bits
Techniques for using random bits in algorithms (probabilistic algorithms)
Implementation of probabilistic algorithms in a computer algebra system
teaching_methods: Self-study with supplementary materials and exercises

assessment_methods.method: Written partial exam 2: Probability in Computer Science

assessment_rules: The module examination consists of two written partial exams. To complete the module, both partial exams must be passed. The first partial exam is a 90-minute exam on Logic. The second partial exam is a 90-minute exam on Probability in Computer Science.
